html:
One of the oldest and longest roads in Asia, running some 3,600 km from Bangladesh across north India and Pakistan to Kabul in Afghanistan. For at least 2,500 years it has linked the Ganges plain with Central Asia. In 1540 to 1545 Sher Shah Suri rebuilt it on a grand scale.

The road follows an ancient route called the Uttarapatha, "the northern road". The Maurya Empire kept up a royal road along it in the 3rd century BCE, running from the Ganges to the northwest past cities such as Taxila. Armies, merchants, pilgrims and ideas travelled it in both directions for centuries.

Sher Shah, who ruled north India for only five years, rebuilt the road from Sonargaon in Bengal to the northwest. Along it he built sarais, rest houses with wells, at regular intervals, planted shade trees, and ran a horse relay that carried news and government orders quickly. The road helped him collect taxes and move troops, and together with his silver rupiya it tied his realm together.

The Mughals kept the road up and marked distances with tall pillars called kos minars, some of which still stand. The British rebuilt it as a paved highway from the 1830s and gave it its English name. Rudyard Kipling, in his novel Kim, called it a river of life.

In 1947, during the Partition of India, huge columns of refugees walked along it in both directions. Today much of it is part of the national highways of the four countries it crosses.
